title: Traffic steering profiles and failover playbook
content:
Summary:
A compact playbook and configuration reference for multi-region traffic steering. Covers three operational profiles (low-latency local-preference, cost-optimized regional pooling, aggressive failover), recommended control-plane components, TTL/health-check defaults, and a runbook for common failure modes. This doc focuses on practical tradeoffs we should adopt for the next release (Q1 2026) and provides concrete knobs for SREs and infra engineers to tune per-customer routing policies.

Goals:
- Provide deterministic routing behavior for user requests across regions while meeting latency SLOs and cost targets.
- Reduce blast radius from regional failures with predictable automatic failover and safe rollback.
- Offer configurable policy profiles customers can select per-route (or per-customer): latency-priority, cost-priority, highly-available.
- Standardize observability and test cases so policy changes can be validated in staging and rolled out gradually.

Constraints and assumptions:
- We operate in multi-cloud + on-prem mixture; not all regions have identical capacity/instance types.
- Edge CDN exists in front of ingress in some customers; we must coordinate TTL and CNAME behavior.
- BGP Anycast is available in selected regions where we control peering (US-EAST, EU-WEST, AP-SG).
- DNS TTLs are honored by diverse resolvers; lower TTL increases control but raises DNS query cost.

Terminology quick-note:
- Regional affinity: attempt to keep a client's traffic within one region for latency/state locality.
- Failover window: time from detection of outage to traffic shift completion (dependent on TTL + resolver caches).
- Control plane: service that holds active policy, health signals, and issues routing decisions (not the data plane).

Recommended profiles (policy presets):
1) latency-priority
   - Ingress: prefer local region Anycast edge if available; fallback to nearest-region Anycast; final fallback via GeoDNS weighted to next-best region.
   - Health sensitivity: aggressive (detect 5xx or >250ms p95 for 60s).
   - TTL: 30s for GeoDNS (only used as emergency fallback).
   - Use-case: interactive chat, low-latency API endpoints.
2) cost-priority
   - Ingress: GeoDNS weight-based routing favoring cheaper zones (based on dynamic cost score).
   - Health sensitivity: relaxed (fail after sustained 3m degradation or explicit instance health down).
   - TTL: 300s.
   - Use-case: batch embeddings, background jobs.
3) highly-available
   - Ingress: Anycast fronted with GeoDNS regional preference; mirrored origins across at least two regions.
   - Health sensitivity: very aggressive; detect and evict on regional reachability or control-plane heartbeat loss (30s).
   - TTL: 60s.
   - Use-case: enterprise traffic needing SLA and transparent failover.

Control plane components (recommended):
- policy-store (single source of truth for routing policies + profile definitions).
- region-health-aggregator (ingests synthetic checks, production 5xx/latency metrics, BGP health hooks).
- decision-engine (evaluates policies against health signals and emits routing commands to DNS/edge).
- rollout-manager (abstractions for canary/batch updates and automatic rollback).
- audit-log (immutable events for routing decisions).

How decisions are issued (hybrid model):
1) Real-time steering decisions for short-term degradations are pushed to Anycast edge controllers (BGP localpref adjustments or edge instance drains).
2) GeoDNS changes are used for medium-term rebalancing and for routes where Anycast isn't present. TTLs are policy-dependent (see profiles).
3) Long-term capacity changes (draining, region decommission) are scheduled through rollout-manager with staged weight shifts.

Health checks and thresholds (defaults to start with):
- Synthetic ping + app-level health every 10s per region. Mark region degraded if 3/5 consecutive failures.
- Production error rate: trigger when 5xx rate >1% sustained for 60s (latency-priority) or 3m (cost-priority).
- Latency SLO breach: p95 > configured threshold (app-specific) for two consecutive windows (60s).

DNS/Public-facing defaults:
- GeoDNS TTL: 30s (latency), 60s (high-availability), 300s (cost).
- Use CNAME to Anycast endpoints when possible; fallback to A records for direct IPs in non-Anycast regions.
- Record pre-warming: when shifting weight, pre-provision edge instances and mark passing before DNS weight increases.

Anycast recommendations:
- Use Anycast primarily as first-hop ingress to achieve stable low-latency routing.
- Implement per-neighbor BGP localpref manipulation from a central controller to bias traffic toward preferred region without tearing down AS-level connectivity.
- Always include a health-signal tie-in before altering BGP preferences (avoid blackholing).

Example policy snippets (policy-store DSL):
- profile: latency-priority
  preferred_regions: [us-east-1, us-west-2]
  min_capacity: 100rps
  failover_sequence: [anycast-local, anycast-nearest, geodns-weighted]
  dns_ttl: 30
  health_sensitivity: aggressive

Failure scenarios and runbook (operator-facing):
Scenario A: One region (eu-west-1) loses backend autoscaler -> capacity drop causing p95 spike
1) Control plane detects p95 > threshold and capacity < min_capacity; mark region as "degraded".
2) Decision engine issues: a) reduce Anycast localpref for eu-west-1; b) instruct edges to set draining=on; c) increase GeoDNS weight to other healthy region.
3) Notify on-call, open incident with severity P2 (severity mapping in incident playbook).
4) If errors continue for 3m, trigger cross-region failover and runbook to scale victims in new region.

Scenario B: BGP peer outage causes asymmetric routing to one PoP
1) Detect via BGP health hooks + synthetic probes failing from multiple vantage points.
2) Immediately mark affected PoP as unhealthy and shift localpref away.
3) If PoP is only Anycast entry for region, use GeoDNS fallback with short TTL.
4) Post-mortem: collect BGP session logs, netflow, and edge metrics.

Rollback guardrails (safety nets):
- Any change that affects >10% global traffic must be canaried to a small set of customers first (rollout-manager).
- Changes that adjust BGP localpref must be reversible automatically within 60s if error signals spike.
- Maintain a separate emergency-override policy that can force all traffic to a single pre-approved region for short windows.

Observability and SLOs to instrument:
- Per-route p50/p95/p99 latency per-region (ingress -> origin).
- 5xx and client error rates by region and by POP.
- DNS resolution failure rate and latency (resolver-level telemetry if available).
- Anycast reachability: percentage of global requests answered by intended PoP.
- Control-plane decision lag: time from detection to command issuance.

Testing matrix (minimum):
- Chaos tests: blackhole region, BGP session flaps, high-latency injection, DNS cache persistence tests.
- Canary suites: 5% traffic for 24h, validate p95 and 5xx remain within acceptable bands before 50% expansion.
- Performance: measure end-to-end latencies with synthetic agents distributed across providers/regions.

Open questions for architecture review:
- How granular should customer-level policy be? Per-route, per-domain, or per-customer? (ops cost vs flexibility)
- Mechanism for authoritative resolver detection: can we detect resolvers that ignore TTLs quickly and adapt?
- How to synthesize a single global cost score factoring cloud spot + egress + instance price across providers?

Phased implementation plan (high level):
- Phase 0 (Q4 2025): instrumentation + region-health-aggregator prototype; minimal decision engine to emit alerts only.
- Phase 1 (Q1 2026): implement profile presets, integrate with Anycast controller (localpref API), and GeoDNS write API; run internal canary.
- Phase 2 (Q2 2026): rollout-manager, per-customer policy UI in Console, automated rollback triggers.

Action items (owners):
- wire up region-health-aggregator (Marcus Lee) - target: 2025-11-21
- PoC Anycast localpref API + safe revert (Liam Chen) - target: 2025-12-05
- Design policy-store DSL + validation tests (Priya Nair) - target: 2025-11-30
- Create chaos test scenarios for DNS caching (Ana Gomez) - target: 2025-12-12

Appendix: quick knobs reference
- GeoDNS TTL: start 60s for HA, 30s latency-critical, 300s cost-critical.
- Health check cadence: 10s synth / 60s rolling window for aggressive detection.
- Canary size: default 5% global traffic for 24h.

Notes / drafts / TODOs:
- Need to align with networking team on supported BGP primitives across colo partners.
- Consider a lightweight resolver-probing agent to estimate global DNS cache behavior (detect long-lived resolvers).
- Investigate using EDNS Client Subnet hints for better geo resolution where customers opt-in.

References:
- Internal PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/routing/pull/872
- Incident review template: CON-4821
- Prior notes: JIRA PLAT-991

End of doc.
